subtopic_detail: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor induced hyponatraemia in an elderly outpatient
stem:
You are the psychiatry outpatient registrar reviewing a 78 year old woman with recurrent major depressive disorder. She started sertraline 50 mg daily 3 weeks ago. She now reports 5 days of headache, nausea, poor concentration and mild unsteadiness, but no seizures or altered conscious state. She lives alone. She has hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily, ischaemic heart disease on aspirin, atorvastatin. She has no history of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or Addison disease. She takes 1 to 1.5 L water daily. She has no vomiting or diarrhoea.

Investigations show sodium 122 mmol/L (baseline 138 mmol/L 3 weeks ago), potassium 3.8, urea 3.4 mmol/L, creatinine 74 micromol/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 68 mmol/L, thyroid function within normal limits, morning serum cortisol 380 nmol/L. Her volume examination is euvolaemic. She has no other medication that could cause hyponatraemia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic clinically, no oedema, mucous membranes moist, no postural drop, no cognitive impairment on brief bedside cognitive test, Glasgow Coma Score 15
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L (baseline 138), potassium 3.8, urea 3.4, creatinine 74, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 68 mmol/L, thyroid function within normal limits, morning cortisol 380 nmol/L

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management now?

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL over 20 minutes immediately as urgent correction, then continue sertraline and hydrochlorothiazide
options.rationale: 3 percent hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure or altered conscious state; here she has moderate symptoms only. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia

options.text: Continue sertraline and hydrochlorothiazide, add tolvaptan 15 mg oral daily as an aquaretic to correct syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is expensive, off label for selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor induced hyponatraemia in AU, and risks rapid overcorrection; cessation of the causative agents plus fluid restriction is first line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia

options.text: Cease sertraline and hydrochlorothiazide, restrict fluid to 800 mL/day, admit for observation and serial sodium every 6 hours to correct slowly
options.rationale: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor induced hyponatraemia (syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion pattern) is most common in the elderly and within the first 4 weeks of therapy, and is worsened by thiazide diuretic. Management is cessation of both the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and thiazide, fluid restriction (800 mL/day), inpatient monitoring and slow correction (below 8 mmol/L in 24 hours) to avoid osmotic demyelination. Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptoms (seizures, altered conscious state). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia

options.text: Give 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 4 hours plus increase her water intake to 2 L per day to increase urinary sodium loss over time
options.rationale: Isotonic saline in syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion pattern can worsen hyponatraemia because water is retained selectively; increasing water intake also worsens the picture. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia

options.text: Reassure and repeat sodium in one week without stopping any medication or restricting fluid, discuss lifestyle education at general practice next week
options.rationale: Sodium 122 mmol/L with symptoms is significant hyponatraemia requiring intervention today; expectant management is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor induced hyponatraemia is most common in elderly outpatients within the first 4 weeks of therapy and is worsened by concurrent thiazide diuretic. It follows a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion pattern (euvolaemic hyponatraemia with concentrated urine and high urinary sodium, once hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency are excluded). Management is cessation of the offending agents, fluid restriction (typically 800 mL/day), and slow correction (rate below 8 mmol/L in 24 hours) to avoid osmotic demyelination. Hypertonic saline (150 mL of 3 percent over 20 minutes, up to 3 doses) is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, altered conscious state). Rechallenge with a different antidepressant class (mirtazapine, agomelatine) can be considered.
key_points: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor hyponatraemia is most common in the elderly within 4 weeks, worsened by thiazide.
Management: cease the drugs, fluid restriction 800 mL/day, correct below 8 mmol/L in 24 hours.
3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL over 20 minutes is reserved for severe symptoms (seizure, altered conscious state).
explanation.pearls: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor plus thiazide induced hyponatraemia in the elderly with moderate symptoms: cease both drugs, fluid restrict to 800 mL/day, admit for monitoring and correct below 8 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid osmotic demyelination.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyponatraemia
European Society of Endocrinology Clinical Practice Guideline on Hyponatraemia

subtopic_detail: Parenteral thiamine dosing for Wernicke encephalopathy prevention in alcohol dependent admission
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar admitting a 52 year old man for alcohol withdrawal management. He drinks approximately 30 standard drinks per day for the last 10 years. He has last had alcohol 8 hours ago. He has no confusion, no ophthalmoplegia and no ataxia. He is not vomiting. He has a poor diet with reduced intake for months and reports 6 kg weight loss over 3 months. He is not currently pregnant (male patient). He has no known thiamine allergy. He has no history of Wernicke encephalopathy. He has been given a benzodiazepine oral loading dose (diazepam 20 mg) for early Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol score 12.

He is otherwise well. His liver function tests show alanine aminotransferase 78 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 132 U/L, gamma glutamyl transferase 320 U/L, mean corpuscular volume 104 fL, platelets 128 x10^9/L, international normalised ratio 1.2, glucose 5.2 mmol/L. Blood alcohol level 0.28 percent. Head computed tomography is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Coarse tremor, mild diaphoresis, no ophthalmoplegia, no nystagmus, gait normal, oriented, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.2 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6, magnesium 0.72 mmol/L, phosphate 0.9 mmol/L, blood alcohol 0.28 percent, computed tomography head normal, liver function tests raised alanine aminotransferase 78 aspartate aminotransferase 132 gamma glutamyl transferase 320

lead_in: Which parenteral thiamine regimen is the most appropriate Wernicke prophylaxis?

options.text: Oral thiamine 100 mg twice daily plus a multivitamin capsule as the primary preventive regimen at emergency triage and continue as an inpatient
options.rationale: Oral thiamine has limited absorption particularly in malnutrition and alcohol dependence; parenteral thiamine is required for Wernicke prophylaxis in this risk profile. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Intramuscular thiamine 100 mg daily for 3 days, then oral thiamine 100 mg daily indefinitely at general practice level for maintenance therapy
options.rationale: Intramuscular 100 mg daily is inadequate prevention in alcohol dependent malnourished patients; intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily is the preventive dose. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Intramuscular multivitamin injection weekly for 4 weeks as monotherapy without additional thiamine dosing during the current admission period
options.rationale: Multivitamin injection does not deliver adequate thiamine dose for Wernicke prophylaxis in alcohol dependent malnourished admissions; specific high dose parenteral thiamine is required. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Intravenous glucose 50 percent 50 mL immediately, then intravenous thiamine 100 mg after the glucose to normalise energy reserves rapidly
options.rationale: Glucose before thiamine can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy in thiamine deficient patients; thiamine must precede or accompany glucose. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

options.text: Intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days, then 300 mg oral daily; treat Wernicke if diagnosed with 500 mg three times daily
options.rationale: For Wernicke prophylaxis in an alcohol dependent malnourished admission, the Australian guidelines recommend intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days followed by oral thiamine 300 mg daily. Established Wernicke encephalopathy is treated with intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily for at least 3 days. Thiamine is given before or with any glucose to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. (Source: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems)
source_refs: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems

explanation.summary: Wernicke encephalopathy is a preventable emergency in alcohol dependent malnourished patients. The Australian guidelines recommend parenteral thiamine 300 mg three times daily intravenously for 3 to 5 days followed by oral thiamine 300 mg daily as prophylaxis in alcohol dependent malnourished admissions. Established Wernicke encephalopathy (any 2 of oculomotor abnormalities, cerebellar dysfunction, altered mental state and dietary deficiency) is treated with intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily for at least 3 days, then 300 mg oral daily. Thiamine must be given before or with any glucose infusion to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy. Magnesium replacement is essential for thiamine efficacy.
key_points: Wernicke prophylaxis in alcohol dependence: intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days, then 300 mg oral daily.
Established Wernicke encephalopathy: intravenous thiamine 500 mg three times daily for at least 3 days.
Thiamine must precede or accompany glucose; correct magnesium concurrently.
explanation.pearls: Alcohol dependent malnourished admission Wernicke prophylaxis: intravenous thiamine 300 mg three times daily for 3 to 5 days, then oral thiamine 300 mg daily; give before or with any glucose and correct magnesium.

sources.label: Australian Guidelines for the Treatment of Alcohol Problems
Royal College of Physicians London guideline on Wernicke encephalopathy

subtopic_detail: Acute pericarditis diagnosis and first line management in an outpatient adult
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 32 year old man with 3 days of central chest pain. The pain is sharp, pleuritic, worse when supine, and relieved by leaning forward. He had a viral upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago. He has no fever, no dyspnoea and no leg swelling. He does not smoke and has no cardiovascular risk factors. He has no personal or family history of ischaemic heart disease. He is on no medication.

Examination reveals a scratchy triphasic pericardial rub audible at the left sternal edge with the patient leaning forward. Cardiovascular examination is otherwise normal. Electrocardiogram shows diffuse concave upward ST elevation with PR segment depression in the inferior and lateral leads, and PR elevation in aVR. High sensitivity troponin I is normal. Chest X ray shows a normal cardiac silhouette. C reactive protein is 68 mg/L, white cell count 9 x10^9/L. Echocardiogram shows no pericardial effusion. Blood pressure is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, comfortable when leaning forward, pericardial friction rub at left sternal edge, no jugular venous distension, heart sounds normal
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram diffuse concave ST elevation with PR depression and PR elevation in aVR, high sensitivity troponin I normal, C reactive protein 68 mg/L, chest X ray normal cardiac silhouette, echocardiogram no pericardial effusion

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered, plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months, and activity restriction
options.rationale: First line therapy for acute idiopathic viral pericarditis is a non steroidal anti inflammatory (ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered) plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months (halves recurrence risk). Activity restriction (no strenuous exercise) is recommended until symptoms resolve and inflammatory markers normalise. Corticosteroids are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or recurrence. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg 6 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks, then tapered, plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months, plus outpatient echocardiogram
options.rationale: Aspirin 300 mg 6 hourly is acceptable but ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly is preferred for non myocardial infarction related acute pericarditis in Australian guidance. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 4 weeks tapered over 4 weeks plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months, plus activity restriction
options.rationale: Corticosteroids as first line are associated with increased recurrence risk; they are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or refractory disease. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Oral paracetamol 1 g 4 to 6 hourly as monotherapy for 4 weeks plus activity restriction and repeat electrocardiogram in 2 weeks
options.rationale: Paracetamol alone is inadequate for acute pericarditis; a non steroidal anti inflammatory plus colchicine is standard first line. (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

options.text: Intravenous heparin bolus 5000 units then infusion at 1000 units/hour targeted to activated partial thromboplastin time as first line
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in acute pericarditis because of haemopericardium and tamponade risk unless independently indicated (e.g. established mechanical valve). (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases)
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases

explanation.summary: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed by at least 2 of pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, new widespread ST elevation with PR depression (and PR elevation in aVR), and new or worsening pericardial effusion; elevated C reactive protein supports the diagnosis. First line therapy for idiopathic viral pericarditis is a non steroidal anti inflammatory (ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered) plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months, which halves recurrence risk. Corticosteroids are reserved for non steroidal anti inflammatory contraindication, colchicine intolerance, autoimmune cause, or refractory disease. Activity restriction until symptoms and inflammatory markers normalise. Anticoagulation is generally avoided because of haemopericardium risk.
key_points: Acute pericarditis: any 2 of pleuritic pain, pericardial rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, or new pericardial effusion.
First line: ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months.
Avoid corticosteroids first line and anticoagulation because of haemopericardium and recurrence risk.
explanation.pearls: Acute idiopathic viral pericarditis: ibuprofen 600 mg 8 hourly for 1 to 2 weeks then tapered plus colchicine 500 microg twice daily for 3 months; activity restriction until inflammatory markers normalise.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology Guideline on Diagnosis and Management of Pericardial Diseases
Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular: Pericarditis

subtopic_detail: Adult male iron deficiency anaemia requires evaluation for occult gastrointestinal blood loss
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 55 year old man referred by his general practitioner with new iron deficiency anaemia noted on routine bloods. He reports mild fatigue and dyspnoea on strenuous exertion but no chest pain, no melaena, no haematemesis and no per rectal bleeding. He has no dysphagia. He has had no recent aspirin or non steroidal anti inflammatory use. He has no personal or family history of colorectal cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease. He is not vegetarian. He drinks 4 standard drinks per week. He does not smoke.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 96 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, mean corpuscular haemoglobin 24 pg, red cell distribution width 18 percent, platelets 460 x10^9/L. Iron studies confirm ferritin 8 microg/L, transferrin saturation 4 percent. Coeliac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA) is negative. Urinalysis is negative for blood. Faecal occult blood testing is not available immediately.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild conjunctival pallor, no lymphadenopathy, no organomegaly, no abdominal masses, per rectal examination normal without palpable rectal mass or melaena
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L, mean corpuscular volume 72 fL, ferritin 8 microg/L, transferrin saturation 4 percent, platelets 460, coeliac serology negative, urinalysis negative for blood

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to identify the source of iron loss?

options.text: Contrast enhanced computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis to identify occult solid organ pathology as first line investigation instead
options.rationale: Computed tomography imaging is less sensitive for mucosal lesions than endoscopy; bidirectional endoscopy is first line. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Faecal occult blood testing as a screening test and defer endoscopy investigation unless the faecal occult blood test returns positive result
options.rationale: In confirmed iron deficiency anaemia, faecal occult blood testing does not obviate the need for endoscopy because the sensitivity is inadequate to exclude significant pathology. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Capsule endoscopy first line to visualise the small bowel because it is a common site of angiodysplasia in adult male iron deficiency anaemia
options.rationale: Capsule endoscopy is a second line investigation after negative bidirectional endoscopy in iron deficiency anaemia, not first line. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Empirical oral iron 100 mg elemental daily for 12 weeks and rescreen haemoglobin, defer endoscopy until iron replacement is completed
options.rationale: Empirical iron replacement without investigation risks missing a colorectal cancer or other treatable pathology; bidirectional endoscopy is the standard investigation in adult male iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

options.text: Bidirectional endoscopy (upper endoscopy and colonoscopy) as urgent outpatient investigations at the same admission or timeframe
options.rationale: In an adult male with new iron deficiency anaemia, current gastroenterology guidance recommends bidirectional endoscopy (upper endoscopy plus colonoscopy) as the initial investigation to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss (peptic ulcer, gastric cancer, coeliac disease if serology equivocal, colorectal cancer, angiodysplasia). Faecal occult blood testing does not obviate the need for endoscopy in confirmed iron deficiency anaemia. (Source: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia)
source_refs: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia

explanation.summary: In an adult male with new iron deficiency anaemia, current gastroenterology guidance recommends bidirectional endoscopy (upper endoscopy plus colonoscopy) as the initial investigation to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss. Common findings include colorectal cancer, gastric cancer, peptic ulcer, oesophagitis, angiodysplasia and coeliac disease. Coeliac serology is checked first; capsule endoscopy is second line if bidirectional endoscopy is negative. Oral iron replacement (100 mg elemental daily or alternate days for enhanced absorption) is started concurrently. Postmenopausal women follow the same pathway; premenopausal women with typical menstrual loss can be managed with iron replacement and clinical review.
key_points: Adult male iron deficiency anaemia: bidirectional endoscopy first line.
Coeliac serology first; capsule endoscopy second line if bidirectional endoscopy negative.
Start oral iron 100 mg elemental daily concurrently (or alternate days to enhance absorption).
explanation.pearls: Adult male new iron deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 96, ferritin 8): bidirectional endoscopy (upper and colonoscopy) as first line to identify occult gastrointestinal blood loss; start oral iron 100 mg elemental daily concurrently.

sources.label: British Society of Gastroenterology Guideline on Iron Deficiency Anaemia
Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal: Iron deficiency anaemia

subtopic_detail: Differentiating Graves disease from subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman with 5 weeks of palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor and 4 kg weight loss. She has no dysphagia and no eye symptoms. She has a soft diffuse enlargement of the thyroid on palpation with no discrete nodule and no tenderness. Auscultation of the thyroid demonstrates a bruit. She has no recent viral illness, no recent iodine load and no amiodarone exposure. She takes no medication. She is not currently pregnant. She has no personal or family history of autoimmune disease.

Thyroid function tests demonstrate thyroid stimulating hormone <0.01 mU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 45 pmol/L (10-25), free triiodothyronine 18 pmol/L (3.5-6.5). Thyroid receptor antibodies are positive at 4.8 IU/L. C reactive protein is 6 mg/L. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm/hour. Beta human chorionic gonadotropin is negative. She has no contraindication to methimazole or radioactive iodine.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 /min, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.0 degC
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor of outstretched hands, warm moist palms, diffuse smooth non tender goitre with audible thyroid bruit, no palpable nodule, no exophthalmos, no lid lag
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone <0.01, free thyroxine 45 pmol/L, free triiodothyronine 18 pmol/L, thyroid receptor antibodies positive 4.8 IU/L, C reactive protein 6, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 12

lead_in: Which feature most strongly favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis?

options.text: Elevated free thyroxine at 45 pmol/L is a feature that alone favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
options.rationale: Elevated free thyroxine is common to both conditions and does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Positive thyroid receptor antibodies plus audible thyroid bruit favour Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
options.rationale: The most useful discriminators between Graves disease and subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment are positive thyroid receptor antibodies and clinical features of Graves specific pathology (audible thyroid bruit reflecting hypervascularity, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema). Subacute thyroiditis characteristically has a tender thyroid, an elevated C reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and low uptake on technetium 99m or iodine 123 thyroid scan. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Weight loss of 4 kg over 5 weeks is a feature that alone favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
options.rationale: Weight loss occurs in any thyrotoxicosis and does not discriminate Graves from subacute thyroiditis. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Diffuse smooth goitre on palpation is a feature that alone favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis at initial assessment
options.rationale: Diffuse smooth goitre is common in Graves disease but is also seen in Hashimoto and subacute thyroiditis; alone it does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

options.text: Suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone at <0.01 mU/L is a feature that alone favours Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis at assessment
options.rationale: Suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone is common to any thyrotoxicosis regardless of cause and does not discriminate. (Source: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

explanation.summary: Graves disease is differentiated from subacute thyroiditis by autoimmune features (positive thyroid receptor antibodies), audible thyroid bruit reflecting hypervascularity, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxoedema and elevated radioactive iodine uptake on scan. Subacute thyroiditis characteristically has a tender thyroid, elevated C reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, low uptake on thyroid scan, and follows a viral upper respiratory tract infection. Graves is treated with methimazole 20 to 40 mg daily titrated (avoid in first trimester where propylthiouracil is preferred), radioactive iodine ablation or thyroidectomy. Subacute thyroiditis is treated symptomatically with a non steroidal anti inflammatory or corticosteroid if severe, and beta blocker for symptom control. Both are followed by hypothyroidism in some cases.
key_points: Graves: thyroid receptor antibodies positive, thyroid bruit, ophthalmopathy, high thyroid scan uptake.
Subacute thyroiditis: tender thyroid, high inflammatory markers, low thyroid scan uptake, post viral.
Radioactive iodine uptake on scan is the definitive imaging discriminator; contraindicated in pregnancy.
explanation.pearls: Positive thyroid receptor antibodies and thyroid bruit favour Graves disease over subacute thyroiditis; thyroid scan (high uptake in Graves, low uptake in thyroiditis) is definitive and is contraindicated in pregnancy.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines Endocrinology: Hyperthyroidism

subtopic_detail: Transient ischaemic attack risk stratification and initiation of dual antiplatelet therapy
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68 year old man with a witnessed 20 minute episode of right sided face and arm weakness with expressive dysphasia that resolved completely by the time of your review. It occurred 6 hours ago. He has hypertension on perindopril and type 2 diabetes on metformin. His baseline blood pressure at his general practitioner has been 150/92 mmHg for the last 3 months. Blood pressure today is 178/98 mmHg. He is right handed and lives independently.

Investigations show glucose 6.4 mmol/L, haemoglobin A1c 7.2 percent, creatinine 92 micromol/L, computed tomography head no acute infarct and no haemorrhage, computed tomography angiogram of carotid arteries reveals a 40 percent left internal carotid artery stenosis. Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm. He is not currently on antithrombotic therapy. He has no known allergies. He has no bleeding history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 178/98 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Fully resolved neurology, no residual weakness or dysphasia, cranial nerves intact, gait normal, no carotid bruit, no atrial fibrillation on prolonged auscultation
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.4, haemoglobin A1c 7.2%, creatinine 92, computed tomography head negative for acute infarct and no haemorrhage, computed tomography angiogram 40% left internal carotid artery stenosis, electrocardiogram sinus rhythm

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate immediate secondary prevention regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily as monotherapy from day 1 lifelong plus continued perindopril and referral to a specialist stroke clinic for planned review
options.rationale: In a high risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 score 6, with speech deficit, weakness, hypertension, diabetes, age), current guidance is a 21 day course of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin plus clopidogrel started immediately, then switch to single antiplatelet therapy. Aspirin monotherapy alone is not preferred for the first 21 days after a high risk transient ischaemic attack. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 300 mg loading then 75 mg daily for 21 days then single agent, plus statin
options.rationale: In high risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 score 4 or above), current Australian Stroke Foundation guidance is to start dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 300 mg loading then 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 300 mg loading then 75 mg daily) for 21 days followed by single antiplatelet therapy long term, plus a high intensity statin (atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg daily), tight blood pressure control (target below 130/80 mmHg long term), lifestyle modification and imaging for extracranial and intracranial vessels. His carotid stenosis 40 percent does not meet surgical revascularisation threshold. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Warfarin loading with international normalised ratio 2 to 3 plus aspirin 100 mg daily long term to reduce recurrent transient ischaemic attack risk
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is reserved for cardioembolic causes (atrial fibrillation, mechanical valve); he is in sinus rhythm without a cardioembolic source and antiplatelet is standard. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Left carotid endarterectomy within 14 days as immediate first line treatment because he has a symptomatic internal carotid artery stenosis
options.rationale: Symptomatic carotid endarterectomy is indicated for 50 to 99 percent symptomatic stenosis (with greater benefit at 70 to 99 percent); his 40 percent stenosis does not meet threshold. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg (10 percent bolus, 90 percent over 60 minutes) as thrombolysis within a 4.5 hour treatment window today
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is for confirmed acute ischaemic stroke with a persisting neurological deficit; a transient ischaemic attack has resolved and does not benefit from thrombolysis. (Source: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management)
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management

explanation.summary: The ABCD2 score risk stratifies transient ischaemic attack (Age >=60, Blood pressure >=140/90, Clinical features [unilateral weakness 2, speech disturbance without weakness 1], Duration [>=60 min 2, 10 to 59 min 1], Diabetes) with scores 4 or above considered high risk of early recurrent stroke. Current Australian Stroke Foundation guidance for high risk transient ischaemic attack is dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) for 21 days then single antiplatelet therapy long term, plus a high intensity statin, tight blood pressure control (target below 130/80 mmHg long term), lifestyle modification, imaging for extracranial and intracranial vessels, and echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring for cardioembolism. Carotid endarterectomy is offered for symptomatic 50 to 99 percent stenosis within 14 days.
key_points: High risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 >=4): dual antiplatelet therapy for 21 days then single agent long term.
Add high intensity statin (atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg), tight blood pressure control (<130/80 long term).
Symptomatic carotid endarterectomy for 50 to 99 percent stenosis within 14 days.
explanation.pearls: High risk transient ischaemic attack (ABCD2 6, resolved weakness with dysphasia): aspirin plus clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy loaded then continued for 21 days then single agent, plus atorvastatin 40 to 80 mg and blood pressure target below 130/80 mmHg.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation Australia Clinical Guidelines for Stroke Management
American Heart Association guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke and TIA

subtopic_detail: Hepatic encephalopathy escalation to rifaximin after lactulose in cirrhosis
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 62 year old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis (Child Pugh C) admitted for the third episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy in the last 4 months. He has been abstinent for 6 months. He is on furosemide 40 mg daily, spironolactone 100 mg daily, propranolol 40 mg twice daily and lactulose 30 mL three times daily titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day, which he takes reliably. There is no gastrointestinal bleed on this admission (haemoglobin stable). He has no infection (blood cultures, urine culture, ascitic tap negative). He has no constipation.

He is currently West Haven grade 2 (mild confusion, asterixis, disoriented in time). Ammonia is 118 micromol/L. Sodium 132, creatinine 88, international normalised ratio 1.7, platelets 78 x10^9/L, magnesium 0.72 mmol/L. He has no active peptic ulcer disease. He is not eligible for liver transplantation because of persistent alcohol use documented in his general practice records within 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.9 degC
data_table.Examination: Mildly jaundiced, spider naevi, palmar erythema, tense ascites, asterixis, orientated to person but not time, Glasgow Coma Score 14
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 118 micromol/L, sodium 132, creatinine 88, international normalised ratio 1.7, platelets 78, magnesium 0.72, ascitic tap no evidence of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, urine and blood cultures negative

lead_in: Which addition is most appropriate for prevention of further overt hepatic encephalopathy?

options.text: Cease lactulose because it has not prevented the third episode, and switch to sodium benzoate 5 g orally twice daily as the alternative agent
options.rationale: Sodium benzoate has limited evidence for hepatic encephalopathy prophylaxis compared with rifaximin; lactulose is continued and rifaximin added as combination therapy. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add oral neomycin 500 mg 6 hourly indefinitely as secondary prophylaxis in place of rifaximin to reduce ammonia levels over the coming weeks
options.rationale: Oral neomycin was previously used but is limited by ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity with prolonged use; rifaximin is preferred. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add oral metronidazole 400 mg twice daily indefinitely as secondary prophylaxis in place of rifaximin to reduce ammonia levels over the coming weeks
options.rationale: Metronidazole carries a risk of peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and is not standard secondary prophylaxis for hepatic encephalopathy. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Add rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily indefinitely as secondary prophylaxis alongside continued titrated lactulose therapy at the same dose
options.rationale: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily added to lactulose is the standard secondary prophylaxis after a second episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy while on adequate lactulose. It reduces recurrence by around 50 percent in trials and is subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme in AU for this indication in patients with cirrhosis with previous hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose is continued titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools per day. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

options.text: Restrict dietary protein to 0.5 g/kg/day indefinitely to reduce ammoniagenesis in the gut and to reduce recurrent hepatic encephalopathy risk
options.rationale: Protein restriction is not recommended in cirrhosis; adequate protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day maintains muscle mass which itself metabolises ammonia. (Source: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis)
source_refs: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis

explanation.summary: Secondary prophylaxis of overt hepatic encephalopathy in cirrhosis after a second episode is achieved by adding rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily to titrated lactulose (2 to 3 soft stools per day). Rifaximin reduces recurrence by around 50 percent and is subsidised on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme in AU for this indication. Protein restriction is not recommended; adequate protein intake (1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day) preserves muscle mass which metabolises ammonia. Identify and treat precipitants (infection, gastrointestinal bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, drugs) at every episode. Liver transplantation is considered where alcohol abstinence and other transplant criteria are met.
key_points: Rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily is added to lactulose after a second overt hepatic encephalopathy episode.
Rifaximin reduces recurrence by around 50 percent; Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme subsidised for this indication in AU.
Do not restrict dietary protein; adequate protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day preserves muscle mass.
explanation.pearls: Recurrent overt hepatic encephalopathy on titrated lactulose in cirrhosis: add rifaximin 550 mg orally twice daily as secondary prophylaxis; maintain protein 1.2 to 1.5 g/kg/day; treat precipitants at every episode.

sources.label: EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Decompensated Cirrhosis
Therapeutic Guidelines Gastrointestinal: Hepatic encephalopathy

subtopic_detail: Discriminating primary biliary cholangitis from primary sclerosing cholangitis in cholestatic derangement
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 52 year old woman with 6 months of fatigue and pruritus. Recent liver function tests show alkaline phosphatase 480 U/L (normal <110), gamma glutamyl transferase 380 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 65 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 58 U/L, bilirubin 22 micromol/L. She has no jaundice. She has no history of inflammatory bowel disease. She has not travelled overseas recently. She takes no medication. She does not drink alcohol. She has no hepatitis B or C exposure (serology negative). She has no family history of autoimmune disease.

Antimitochondrial antibody is positive at high titre. Antinuclear antibody is positive at 1:160 with a nuclear rim pattern. Immunoglobulin M is raised at 5.2 g/L. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrates a normal biliary tree without strictures or beading. Colonoscopy from 12 months ago demonstrated no colitis and was normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Fatigued, mild scratch marks over the arms and back, no jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no splenomegaly, no ascites, no encephalopathy signs
data_table.Investigations: Alkaline phosphatase 480, gamma glutamyl transferase 380, alanine aminotransferase 65, aspartate aminotransferase 58, bilirubin 22, antimitochondrial antibody positive high titre, immunoglobulin M raised, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography normal biliary tree

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and first line disease modifying therapy?

options.text: Primary biliary cholangitis, treat with ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily and monitor treatment response at 12 months on liver function
options.rationale: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by cholestatic liver function tests with alkaline phosphatase 1.5 times upper limit of normal or above for at least 6 months, positive antimitochondrial antibody (or specific antinuclear antibodies with nuclear rim pattern in seronegative cases) and compatible liver biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain. First line disease modifying therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg orally daily, with treatment response defined by biochemical response (alkaline phosphatase falling below defined thresholds) at 12 months (POISE, GLOBE and UK-PBC risk calculators). Obeticholic acid or bezafibrate is added for inadequate response. Pruritus is treated with cholestyramine 4 g twice daily and second line rifampicin. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Primary sclerosing cholangitis, treat with ursodeoxycholic acid 15 mg/kg daily plus colonoscopy every 12 months for inflammatory bowel disease screen
options.rationale: Primary sclerosing cholangitis has a beaded biliary tree on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease; her cholangiogram is normal. Antimitochondrial antibody positive high titre with elevated immunoglobulin M is diagnostic of primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Autoimmune hepatitis, treat with prednisolone 30 mg daily tapering plus azathioprine 1 to 2 mg/kg daily once thiopurine methyltransferase confirmed
options.rationale: Autoimmune hepatitis typically has a hepatitic pattern (elevated alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase) with positive smooth muscle antibody and elevated immunoglobulin G, not the cholestatic pattern with positive antimitochondrial antibody and elevated immunoglobulin M seen here. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: Non alcoholic fatty liver disease, initiate lifestyle intervention with a 10 percent weight loss target and glucose lowering therapy at general practice
options.rationale: Non alcoholic fatty liver disease is typically hepatitic and does not produce this magnitude of cholestasis with positive antimitochondrial antibody; imaging would show steatosis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

options.text: IgG4 related sclerosing cholangitis, treat with prednisolone 40 mg daily and rituximab 375 mg/m^2 for those with steroid failure at 3 months
options.rationale: IgG4 related sclerosing cholangitis usually shows bile duct strictures on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography with elevated IgG4; her cholangiogram is normal and her antibody profile fits primary biliary cholangitis. (Source: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis)
source_refs: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

explanation.summary: Primary biliary cholangitis is diagnosed by cholestatic liver function tests with alkaline phosphatase 1.5 times upper limit of normal or above for at least 6 months, positive antimitochondrial antibody (or specific antinuclear antibodies with nuclear rim or multiple nuclear dot patterns in seronegative cases), and compatible liver biopsy if diagnosis is uncertain. First line disease modifying therapy is ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg orally daily, with treatment response assessed at 12 months using validated biochemical response criteria (POISE, GLOBE, UK-PBC). Second line is obeticholic acid or bezafibrate for inadequate response. Pruritus is treated with cholestyramine 4 g twice daily then rifampicin second line. Primary sclerosing cholangitis in contrast has a beaded biliary tree, is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, and has no proven disease modifying therapy (though ursodeoxycholic acid is often trialled).
key_points: Primary biliary cholangitis: cholestatic liver function tests plus positive antimitochondrial antibody plus elevated immunoglobulin M.
First line: ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily; response assessed at 12 months.
Pruritus first line: cholestyramine 4 g twice daily; second line: rifampicin.
explanation.pearls: Cholestatic pattern (alkaline phosphatase 480) with positive antimitochondrial antibody and normal magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography is primary biliary cholangitis; start ursodeoxycholic acid 13 to 15 mg/kg daily and reassess biochemical response at 12 months.

sources.label: AASLD Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline on Primary Biliary Cholangitis

subtopic_detail: Amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 1 versus type 2 differentiation and management
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 68 year old man on amiodarone 200 mg daily for the last 3 years for symptomatic paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. He presents with 6 weeks of palpitations, weight loss and heat intolerance. His atrial fibrillation has become persistent and rate is difficult to control despite bisoprolol. He has ischaemic heart disease with prior anterior myocardial infarction and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 38 percent, and mild chronic kidney disease. He has no personal or family history of thyroid disease. He has not had recent iodine load beyond amiodarone.

Thyroid function shows thyroid stimulating hormone <0.01 mU/L, free thyroxine 62 pmol/L, free triiodothyronine 12 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative. Interleukin 6 is elevated. Thyroid ultrasound shows a normal sized thyroid with hyperechoic parenchyma but absent Doppler flow (very low vascularity). He cannot have technetium 99m uptake scan because of amiodarone iodine load blocking uptake. His cardiologist is concerned that stopping amiodarone will worsen his arrhythmia.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 /min irregularly irregular, blood pressure 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.2 degC
data_table.Examination: Fine tremor, warm palms, thin, no clinically palpable goitre, no eye signs, atrial fibrillation on cardiac auscultation with variable murmur intensity
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone <0.01, free thyroxine 62 pmol/L, free triiodothyronine 12 pmol/L, thyroid receptor antibodies negative, interleukin 6 elevated, thyroid ultrasound normal size with hyperechoic parenchyma and absent Doppler flow, technetium 99m uptake very low

lead_in: Which is the most likely subtype and most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis, treat with prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months, discuss amiodarone continuation with cardiology
options.rationale: Type 2 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis is a destructive thyroiditis identified by absent Doppler flow on ultrasound, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6, and follows a self limiting course with an eventual hypothyroid phase. First line treatment is oral prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months. Cessation of amiodarone is discussed with cardiology (the drug is only marginally responsible for continuing destructive thyroiditis but ceasing removes ongoing thyroid injury; balancing arrhythmia risk against thyroid effect is essential). Type 1 in contrast is iodine induced Graves or toxic multinodular goitre, has increased Doppler flow, positive antibodies, and is treated with thionamide plus potassium perchlorate. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Type 1 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis, treat with carbimazole 40 mg daily plus potassium perchlorate 200 mg 6 hourly and continue amiodarone
options.rationale: Type 1 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis features increased Doppler flow on ultrasound and positive thyroid receptor antibodies; this pattern (absent Doppler, negative antibodies, elevated interleukin 6) fits type 2, which is a destructive thyroiditis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Mixed type amiodarone thyrotoxicosis, treat with combination carbimazole 40 mg daily plus prednisolone 40 mg daily plus lithium 800 mg daily
options.rationale: Mixed type is treated with combination of thionamide plus corticosteroid when the type cannot be differentiated; here the pattern is clearly type 2 (absent Doppler, negative antibodies, high interleukin 6) so combination therapy is not required first line. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis, treat with ibuprofen 400 mg 6 hourly and continue amiodarone as the causative agent has not been identified
options.rationale: Subacute thyroiditis follows a viral prodrome and features tender thyroid and elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; this is amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis type 2 rather than subacute thyroiditis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

options.text: Factitious thyrotoxicosis from unrecognised exogenous thyroxine, review medication list and cease all thyroid hormone therapy immediately
options.rationale: Factitious thyrotoxicosis features low thyroglobulin and low iodine uptake without clinical goitre changes; his ultrasound and interleukin 6 fit type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis. (Source: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction)
source_refs: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction

explanation.summary: Amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis divides into type 1 (iodine induced Graves or toxic multinodular goitre, seen on abnormal thyroid substrate) and type 2 (amiodarone induced destructive thyroiditis on normal thyroid substrate). Discriminators favouring type 2 are normal or small thyroid on ultrasound with absent or low Doppler flow, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6, and eventual hypothyroid phase. Type 1 is treated with high dose thionamide (carbimazole 40 to 60 mg daily) plus potassium perchlorate 200 mg 6 hourly, and type 2 with prednisolone 40 mg daily tapered over 3 months; mixed type is treated with combination therapy. Amiodarone cessation is discussed with cardiology and depends on arrhythmia indication. The drug is stored in adipose tissue with a half life of 60 days so cessation does not immediately resolve thyroid effect.
key_points: Type 1 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis: iodine induced Graves or toxic nodular goitre; treat with thionamide plus potassium perchlorate.
Type 2 amiodarone thyrotoxicosis: destructive thyroiditis with absent Doppler, high interleukin 6; treat with prednisolone 40 mg daily.
Amiodarone half life is 60 days; cessation does not immediately resolve thyroid effect.
explanation.pearls: Type 2 amiodarone induced thyrotoxicosis (absent Doppler flow, negative thyroid receptor antibodies, elevated interleukin 6): prednisolone 40 mg orally daily tapered over 3 months; discuss amiodarone continuation with cardiology balancing arrhythmia against thyroid injury.

sources.label: European Thyroid Association Guideline on Amiodarone Induced Thyroid Dysfunction
Endocrine Society Hyperthyroidism Clinical Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Serotonin toxicity grading and management after tramadol plus escitalopram co-prescription
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar reviewing a 64 year old woman presenting 12 hours after starting tramadol 50 mg 6 hourly for post operative pain. She has been on escitalopram 20 mg daily for the last 3 years for major depressive disorder. She is now agitated, febrile with a temperature of 39.4 degrees Celsius, tachycardic 128 /min, hypertensive 178/108 mmHg, and profoundly diaphoretic. Neurological examination demonstrates sustained inducible ankle clonus, hyperreflexia, ocular clonus, tremor of the outstretched hands and hypertonia which is greater in the lower limbs than in the upper limbs. Glasgow Coma Score is 13.

Investigations show creatine kinase 3200 U/L (rising), sodium 138, potassium 4.6, creatinine 118 micromol/L (baseline 76), lactate 3.4 mmol/L, arterial blood gas pH 7.30 base excess -6, computed tomography head is normal. Lumbar puncture has been sent to exclude meningitis. She has no personal history of catatonia, no exposure to antipsychotics and no history of neuroleptic malignant syndrome. She has been in the department for 60 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 178/108 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 39.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Diaphoresis, inducible ankle clonus sustained, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, hypertonia lower more than upper limbs, tremor, Glasgow Coma Score 13
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 3200 U/L, creatinine 118 (baseline 76), lactate 3.4, pH 7.30 base excess -6, computed tomography head normal, lumbar puncture pending

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous dantrolene 1 to 2.5 mg/kg immediately for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome and continue escitalopram and tramadol
options.rationale: This is serotonin toxicity not neuroleptic malignant syndrome (clonus present, no antipsychotic exposure, recent serotonergic drug initiation); dantrolene is not first line here and continuing serotonergic drugs is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Continue escitalopram and tramadol, give oral paracetamol 1 g and ibuprofen 400 mg for fever, admit for observation on the general medical ward
options.rationale: Continuing serotonergic drugs perpetuates and worsens the toxicity; immediate cessation is mandatory. Fever is treated by active cooling and benzodiazepines, not antipyretics because the mechanism is muscular hyperactivity not cytokine mediated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Cease escitalopram alone, continue tramadol, give haloperidol 5 mg intravenously as chemical restraint for the agitation to enable safer nursing care
options.rationale: Tramadol is a serotonergic drug and must also be ceased; haloperidol is contraindicated because it can worsen hyperthermia and lower seizure threshold in this setting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Cease all serotonergic medications, aggressive intravenous cooling and fluids, benzodiazepines for agitation, cyproheptadine 12 mg oral then 2 mg 2 hourly
options.rationale: Serotonin toxicity meeting Hunter criteria (spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia) is treated by immediate cessation of all serotonergic drugs, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, active cooling, benzodiazepines (diazepam 5 to 10 mg intravenously repeated) for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as loading dose then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours as a targeted 5HT2A antagonist. Non depolarising neuromuscular blockade and intensive care admission is required in severe cases. Discriminators from neuroleptic malignant syndrome include clonus (present in serotonin toxicity, absent in neuroleptic malignant syndrome), lower limb greater than upper limb hypertonia, and recent serotonergic drug exposure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg for suspected bacterial meningitis and continue serotonergic drugs during workup
options.rationale: Meningitis is unlikely in the absence of meningism and the clinical picture (clonus, ocular clonus, hyperreflexia, recent tramadol on escitalopram) is serotonin toxicity; cessation of serotonergic drugs and cyproheptadine is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity

explanation.summary: Serotonin toxicity is a clinical diagnosis using Hunter criteria (spontaneous clonus, or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia) after serotonergic drug exposure. Tramadol is a serotonergic opioid and co-prescription with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is a classic trigger. Management is immediate cessation of all serotonergic drugs, aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation, active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation and rigidity, and cyproheptadine 12 mg orally as loading dose then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours. Non depolarising neuromuscular blockade with intubation is required in severe cases (temperature above 41.1 degrees Celsius). Discriminators from neuroleptic malignant syndrome include clonus (present in serotonin toxicity, absent in neuroleptic malignant syndrome) and lower limb greater than upper limb hypertonia.
key_points: Serotonin toxicity Hunter criteria: spontaneous or inducible clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis, or tremor with hyperreflexia.
Management: cease all serotonergic drugs, active cooling, benzodiazepines, cyproheptadine 12 mg loading then 2 mg 2 hourly.
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome vs serotonin toxicity: absence of clonus in neuroleptic malignant syndrome; lead pipe rigidity vs lower more than upper limb hypertonia.
explanation.pearls: Serotonin toxicity from tramadol on escitalopram: cease all serotonergic drugs, active cooling, benzodiazepines for agitation, cyproheptadine 12 mg orally loading then 2 mg 2 hourly up to 32 mg per 24 hours; intensive care admission if temperature above 41.1 degrees Celsius.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and Wilderness: Serotonin toxicity
Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria Australian Journal of Emergency Medicine
